newsitem.title: UK: WPP Group details new media strategy.
newsitem.headline: WPP Group details new media strategy.

text.p: WPP Group Plc, the world's largest advertising and marketing company, has an appetite for one or two more acquisitions after buying a stake in a seventh new media company earlier this week, according to WPP's group director of strategy.
"We've probably got one or two more investments we need to make," Eric Salama told Reuters in an interview. "Probably a Web site development company in the United States would be useful."
Six of the seven media investments that WPP has made to date have been in U.S.-based companies, including the purchase announced Monday of a stake in HyperParallel.

San Francisco-based HyperParallel is a data mining company, helping companies use transactional data to better understand consumer behaviour and the impact of price, brand name and merchandise mix on brand loyalty and spending.

Other U.S. investments include Wired Ventures, an advertising-driven Web magazine; Individual, a customised news service; BroadVision for Internet-based direct marketing; venture capital company Media Technology Ventures, and on-line home shopping firm Peapod.

WPP's only investment in a non-U.S. media venture was made last month in Syzygy, a London-based specialist in strategy, development and marketing of commercial Internet and corporate intranet solutions.
With the exception of Germany, Salama said WPP was not looking at new media investments outside the United States, and he bluntly said the U.S. West Coast was a key focus.
Noting WPP's investment in Media Technology, he said, "It gives us a presence on the West Coast, where you really need to be if you're serious about this business."

Some of WPP's investments, such as the stake in San Francisco-based BroadVision bought last year, give it exposure outside the U.S. market. A software provider for personalised Internet marketing and selling, BroadVision does most of its work in Europe and Asia.
But non-U.S. markets hold little investment appeal. Despite the presence in Asia of some Web site development companies, Salama said, "There's not an awful lot of good things to buy."

WPP, which to date has spent a total of about $15 million on its minority stakes in new media companies, might increase some of those stakes in the future. The existing stakes in the seven companies range from 1 percent to 30 percent.

"There are some companies like Wired and Peapod where I can't imagine it's in our interest to increase the stake substantially," said Salama. "In other cases like HyperParallel, which is much more core to our direct-marketing business, then I could see us over time increasing that stake."

WPP does not see new media as a significant contributor to profits in the near term. "I don't think anyone's going to make huge amounts of money in new media for the next two or three years," said Salama.
But Salama said WPP has taken a clear, strategic approach to new media.

"Advertising itself is the least interesting aspect of new media," he said. "The most interesting are what it can do for the distribution ... cutting out the middlemen. The other aspect is to do with direct marketing. It allows you to take direct marketing to another level in how you interact with your customers."
Unlike traditional direct marketing, the Internet allows users' habits to be closely tracked, monitoring what news stories and other items they read and when they read them.
"The idea itself is not different," said Salama. "The difference is you can do it on a global basis, in real time, and for a fraction of the cost."
